milestone.title: LaserWriter and AppleTalk unveiled, January 23, 1985
milestone.note: Networked PostScript printing became a foundational component of the desktop-publishing revolution.

editorNote: A shared printer, a new office ambition, and games that hand the tools to their players.
morningLine: Apple unveils LaserWriter and AppleTalk; the personal-computer contest gathers pace.

lead.headline: Apple puts a shared laser printer at the center of the Macintosh Office
lead.dek: January 23 unveiling pairs a $6,995 printer with a network; March availability is promised.
body: Apple has placed a shared laser printer at the center of its new Macintosh Office strategy. At its January 23 shareholders meeting in Cupertino, the company presented a system intended to make the Macintosh a stronger contender for office work, with AppleTalk linking desks to a common printing resource.

The LaserWriter carries a $6,995 price tag, rounded to $7,000 in the contemporary newspaper account. AppleTalk connection equipment costs $50; that is a connection-device price, not a quotation for an entire office installation. Apple describes a network of up to 32 computers, or a printer shared by up to 31 Macintoshes.

Printer and networking equipment are scheduled for March, rather than being on sale this week. Links to IBM PCs are promised for the fall. The printer uses Adobe PostScript, putting sophisticated page description into the office-printing proposition.

Software remains a test of the plan. Lotus Jazz, previously expected in January, has slipped to March according to the January 24 report. Apple reports 275,000 Macintosh sales in the preceding year and hopes to sell 10,000 Macintosh Office bundles in 1985; turning that ambition into routine office use will require the applications as well as the wires.

stories.headline: Atari promises Macintosh-style computing without Macintosh prices
body: Atari’s January CES prototypes put a new price challenge before the personal-computer buyer. The announced 520ST combines 512K of memory and an 8 MHz Motorola 68000 with a $599 show price; the 128K 130ST is announced at $399. These are preliminary promises, not machines established as available at the shop counter this week.

Digital Research GEM supplies the familiar vocabulary of icons, windows, menus and a mouse. Announced display choices range from 320 by 200 in 16 colors to 640 by 400 monochrome. MIDI, serial, parallel and disk connections suggest uses stretching from music and games to desk work.

The company promises second-quarter availability, while operating-system and language decisions remain unfinished in the show account. Alongside the ST, the eight-bit XE family seeks existing home-computer buyers: the 64K 65XE is priced at $99 and the 128K 130XE at about $150.

stories.headline: Commodore 128 promises three computers in one
body: Commodore’s January CES proposal is three operating personalities in one machine. The 128 offers Commodore 64 compatibility, a native 128K environment using an 8502 processor, and a Z80A route into CP/M 3.0.

Native mode adds 40- or 80-column text and BASIC 7.0; C64 operation retains BASIC 2.0 and its 40-column display. COMPUTE! staff ran SpeedScript 3.0 in C64 mode at the show, a useful demonstration rather than an exhaustive compatibility verdict.

Price remains unsettled. COMPUTE! records no firm Commodore price announcement, while suggesting under $300 and an April or May introduction. Buyers should treat estimates from the show floor as estimates, not a confirmed retail ticket.

stories.headline: Games invite players to build the tracks, creatures and adventures
body: January’s CES game displays invite players to become designers. Electronic Arts showed Racing Destruction Set, with tracks to construct and cars to race, and Adventure Construction Set, extending the construction-kit idea into adventures. No exact-week release or price is established by the show report.

Creature construction also enters the combat arena in the product the report calls Mail Order Monster. The attraction is not simply another opponent: it is the ability to design a creature and send it into competition. The report describes three levels of combat.

Creative Software brings a different kind of player performance. Trolls and Tribulations sends trolls through dangerous caverns in search of treasure, while Break Street draws on consultation with Seattle’s DeRoxy Crew breakdancers. The home-computer shelf is making room for creation as well as reflexes.

briefs.headline: Macintosh Office must wait for IBM links
briefs.summary: Apple said office-network connections to IBM PCs would not be available until fall; do not present interoperability as already delivered.

briefs.headline: Online college credit at home
briefs.summary: CES report describes Telelearning courses for Apple, IBM and C64 users: course disks and instructor access by modem, $35–$200, with proctored exams required for final credit.

worldAnchor.headline: Cold moves Reagan’s public inauguration indoors
worldAnchor.summary: January 21 diary records moving the ceremony to the Capitol rotunda and canceling the outdoor parade because of below-zero cold; distinguish the public ceremony from January 20 constitutional swearing-in.

bbsNote.headline: 2400 bps is tempting—but the bulletin boards may get there first
bbsNote.summary: Arlan R. Levitan’s January 1985 COMPUTE! column compares modem economics and reports prospective manufacturer support for selected BBS sysops. A January CES report supplies C64 online-game service details.

posts.text: 300 bps modems cost $50–$280; Anchor Automation and Qubie had broken the $300 barrier for 300/1200 bps units; 2400 bps equipment still cost $800–$1,500.

posts.platform: CompuServe / The Source / Delphi / Dow Jones News-Retrieval
posts.text: Levitan reports none of the commercial information services then offered 2400 bps service. His Just Folks example and hourly charges are hypothetical, not real tariff evidence.

The columnist reports several modem manufacturers working with selected popular-board operators on discounted 2400 bps seed programs. No manufacturers or board identities are specified; do not invent names or completed deployments.
Ahl’s January CES report lists email, CB chat, program transfer and online games including backgammon, checkers, chess, bridge and go; $40 initial fee and $6 monthly charge.

curiosity.headline: Infocom turns its CES party into a live murder mystery
curiosity.summary: Adventure-game culture stepped away from the keyboard at January CES.
curiosity.detail: David H. Ahl reports that New York’s Murder-To-Go troupe staged a participatory mystery for Infocom guests, who examined the scene and police reports. Nine guests solved it; the top winner received a trip to Bermuda. This is a CES party anecdote, not a game release.

periodAd.headline: SkiWriter II brings telecommunications to the document
periodAd.summary: Ken Skier’s CES demonstration combines word processing with built-in telecommunications. Listed for C64, PC, PCjr and Apple at $69.95.

market.headline: Faster modems need somewhere to call
market.summary: January COMPUTE! places 300 bps modems at $50–$280 and 2400 bps units at $800–$1,500. Its survey reports no 2400 bps access yet at the major commercial information services; selected BBS sysops are the subject of manufacturer seed-program discussions.
